Summary: For captive primates, puzzle feeders have been associated with increased foraging behaviour and tool use, and more time spent feeding with less time inactive, but also decreased food sharing and increased aggression [1318]. For captive carnivores, providing live invertebrate prey (including via feeding devices) increased explorative behaviours in fennec foxes [1926]. Prey-simulating devices (e.g., lures, pulleys, bungees) increased activity levels and behavioural diversity in felids, with pacing decreasing and walking increasing in cougars; however, pacing initially increased in tigers when provided with a carcass on a bungee [1927].
Statements: ['For captive primates, puzzle feeders have been associated with increased foraging behaviour and tool use.', 'Puzzle feeders for captive primates have been associated with more time spent feeding and less time being inactive.', 'Puzzle feeders for captive primates have been associated with decreased food sharing and increased aggression.', 'Providing live invertebrate prey, including via feeding devices, increased explorative behaviours in captive fennec foxes.', 'Prey-simulating devices increased activity levels and behavioural diversity in felids.', 'The use of prey-simulating devices led to decreased pacing and increased walking in cougars.', 'Pacing initially increased in tigers when tigers were provided with a carcass on a bungee.']

key: cited_stmt_gen___gpt-5__In a zoo environment, what are the documented effects of altering the timing and predictability of feeding schedules for captive primates and carnivores?

Summary: For primates, one replicated controlled study found that shifting to unpredictable feeding schedules decreased inactivity in chimpanzees [1338]. For carnivores, unpredictable or random temporal feeding schedules reduced stereotypic pacing in tigers and cheetahs according to multiple replicated studies, increased territorial behavior in coyotes without affecting traveling or foraging in one replicated before-and-after controlled study, and increased behavioral diversity in red foxes and alertness in a black-footed cat in before-and-after studies [1904]. No studies were found that directly tested altering feeding schedules in relation to visitor activity or the use of automated feeders for carnivores [1914, 1913].
Statements: ['For primates, shifting to unpredictable feeding schedules decreased inactivity in chimpanzees.', 'For carnivores, unpredictable or random temporal feeding schedules reduced stereotypic pacing in tigers and cheetahs.', 'Unpredictable or random temporal feeding schedules increased territorial behavior in coyotes without affecting traveling or foraging.', 'Unpredictable or random temporal feeding schedules increased behavioral diversity in red foxes.', 'Unpredictable or random temporal feeding schedules increased alertness in a black-footed cat.', 'No studies were found that directly tested altering feeding schedules for carnivores in relation to visitor activity.', 'No studies were found that directly tested altering feeding schedules for carnivores in relation to the use of automated feeders.']

Summary: For primates, identified alternatives include presenting whole foods rather than chopped or processed items, which increased amount consumed and time spent feeding in macaques [1323]; offering fresh produce instead of pellet feed, which increased feeding time and reduced inactivity in rhesus macaques [1335]; providing cut branches (browse), with captive gorillas using wild-like processing skills when given stinging nettles [1332]; providing nectar (including artificial nectar), for which no direct quantitative evidence on effects was captured [1331]; and installing live vegetation in planters for foraging, which increased time spent foraging by chimpanzees compared to browse/grass with the normal diet [1327]. For carnivores, alternatives include feeding whole carcasses (with or without organs/gastrointestinal tract), which reduced pacing in lions, leopards, snow leopards and cougars but increased pacing in tigers; in cheetahs, whole rabbit was associated with lower blood protein urea, zinc and vitamin A than supplemented beef and with lower inflammatory bowel indicators; in ocelots and African wildcats, whole young chickens had lower digestible energy/fat and lower organic matter digestibility than commercial or ground-chicken diets [1901]; feeding a plant-derived protein diet, which increased digestible energy and dry matter digestibility but decreased mineral retention and plasma taurine in maned wolves compared to (supplemented) animal-based protein diets [1903]; allocating fast days, which was associated with more pacing on non-feeding days in large felids fed once every three days [1906]; supplementing meat-based diets with vitamins or minerals (no direct quantitative evidence captured) [1907]; and altering food abundance or type seasonally (no direct quantitative evidence captured) [1910].

Summary: Available dietary-related modifications include: providing cut browse such as stinging nettles, which elicited wild-like processing skills in captive gorillas [1332]; planting live vegetation (e.g., rye grass) and scattering seeds in planters to increase time spent foraging [1327]; presenting foods whole rather than chopped, which increased amount consumed and time feeding in macaques [1323]; offering fresh produce instead of pellet feed, which increased feeding time and reduced inactivity in rhesus macaques [1335]; supplying live invertebrate prey, which reduced inactivity and increased foraging to levels seen in wild loris [1333]; providing access to food at all times (day and night), for which no evidence of effects was captured [1340]; providing nectar (including artificial nectar), for which no evidence of effects was captured [1331]; changing the number of feeds per day, which increased feeding time in chimpanzees but was associated with increased hair eating in baboons [1337]; adding gum solutions to drilled hollow feeders, for which no evidence of effects was captured [1326]; and providing food at natural (wild) feeding times, for which no evidence of effects was captured [1339].
Statements: ['Providing cut browse such as stinging nettles is a dietary modification that elicited wild-like processing skills in captive gorillas.', 'Planting live vegetation, like rye grass, and scattering seeds in planters can increase the time captive primates spend foraging.', 'Presenting foods whole rather than chopped increased the amount consumed and the time spent feeding in macaques.', 'Offering fresh produce instead of pellet feed increased feeding time and reduced inactivity in rhesus macaques.', 'Supplying live invertebrate prey to captive loris reduced inactivity and increased foraging to levels seen in wild loris.', 'No evidence of effects was captured for the dietary modification of providing access to food at all times, day and night.', 'No evidence of effects was captured for the dietary modification of providing nectar, including artificial nectar.', 'Changing the number of feeds per day increased feeding time in chimpanzees.', 'Changing the number of feeds per day was associated with increased hair eating in baboons.', 'No evidence of effects was captured for the dietary modification of adding gum solutions to drilled hollow feeders.', 'No evidence of effects was captured for the dietary modification of providing food at natural (wild) feeding times.']

Summary: Benefits reported include increased activity and behavioural diversity in felids when presented with a lure or pulley system [1927], as well as increased exploratory and foraging behaviours and decreased stereotypic behaviours in sloth bears and spectacled bears when food was presented inside objects [1924]. Additional benefits noted were decreased pacing and increased walking in cougars when provided with a carcass on a bungee [1927]. Reported harms or negative outcomes include an initial increase in pacing in tigers when provided with a carcass on a bungee [1927], and a decrease in exploring/foraging behaviours in one sloth bear when presented with food inside objects [1924]. Neutral findings included grizzly bears spending a similar time manipulating food in a box and freely available food [1924].
Statements: ['A reported benefit of using a lure or pulley system for felids is increased activity and behavioural diversity.', 'Increased exploratory and foraging behaviours were reported as a benefit in sloth bears and spectacled bears when food was presented inside objects.', 'Decreased stereotypic behaviours were reported as a benefit in sloth bears and spectacled bears when food was presented inside objects.', 'Decreased pacing was a noted benefit in cougars when the cougars were provided with a carcass on a bungee.', 'Increased walking was a noted benefit in cougars when the cougars were provided with a carcass on a bungee.', 'A reported harm or negative outcome was an initial increase in pacing in tigers when the tigers were provided with a carcass on a bungee.', 'A decrease in exploring and foraging behaviours was a reported negative outcome in one sloth bear when the bear was presented with food inside objects.', 'A neutral finding was that grizzly bears spent a similar amount of time manipulating food in a box and freely available food.']
